source: Marqu - The Hebrew Gospel of Mark v1.2
notes_on_source: Verses 55-56 appear merged in the source text into a single verse 55.

verses.translation: And Yeshua went out{H3318} from there and went{H1980} to his locales, and his disciples followed{H4900} after him.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נכחיותיו (nekhachiyotav — 'his locales/neighborhoods'), a noun formed from נכח (nokhach — 'opposite/in front of', H5227). This is a uniquely Hebrew-constructed word for familiar surroundings. Greek has πατρίδα ('fatherland/hometown'). A back-translator from Greek would use מולדתו (moladto — 'his birthplace') or ארצו (artso — 'his land'), not this unusual formation from נכח.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'his locales' (נכחיותיו). Greek: 'his hometown' (πατρίδα). Different concepts.

verses.translation: And on one{H259} sabbath{H7676} he began to teach{H3925} in the house of assembly{H1004}, and many{H7227} hearing{H8085} were amazed{H8539} at his instruction, saying{H559}: From where has he the wisdom{H2451} given{H5414} to him, and from where the strength{H3581} that goes out{H3318} from his hands{H3027}?

one_way_hebrew: Uses מוסרו (musaro — 'his instruction/discipline', from מוסר H4148). In the OT, מוסר is the wisdom-tradition term for instruction and moral discipline (Prov 1:2,7,8, 3:11, 4:1, 8:33, 12:1). Greek has simply διδαχῇ ('teaching'). A back-translator from Greek would use תורתו or למודו, not the loaded Proverbs-wisdom term מוסר. The Hebrew says the crowd was amazed at his wisdom-tradition instruction.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'strength that goes out from his hands' (כח מהידים יוצא). Greek: δυνάμεις τοιαῦται ('such mighty works'). The Hebrew localizes the power to his hands; Greek speaks of mighty works generally.
Hebrew: 'the wisdom given to him' (passive — wisdom received). Greek: ἡ σοφία ἡ δοθεῖσα τούτῳ (similar, 'given to this one'). Both acknowledge the wisdom comes from outside.
translation_notes: מוסר (musar, H4148) in Proverbs encompasses the full scope of wisdom training: moral correction, intellectual instruction, and character formation. It is far richer than generic 'teaching.'

verses.translation: Is he not the son{H1121} of a certain smith{H5301} and Miriam{H4813}? And his relatives{H7138} are Yaaqov{H3290} and Yosef{H3130} and Yehudah{H3063} and Shimon{H8095}, and all these are with us. And they were offended{H3782} by him.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses בן נפח (ben napach — 'son of a smith/forger'). The word נפח (H5301) means 'to blow' (bellows) and refers to a metalworker/smith. Isaiah 54:16: 'Behold, I created the smith (נפח) who blows the coals in the fire.' Greek has τέκτων (tektōn — 'carpenter/craftsman/builder'). A back-translator from Greek τέκτων would use חרש עצים (charash etsim — 'worker of wood') or simply חרש (artisan). The word נפח specifically means a SMITH — one who works metal by blowing bellows at a forge. Entirely different trade from carpentry.

Uses קרוביו (qerovav — 'his relatives/near ones', from קרב H7138 — 'near'). Greek has ἀδελφοί ('brothers'). A back-translator from 'brothers' would use אחיו (echav — 'his brothers'). The Hebrew uses the broader kinship term קרובים, which encompasses cousins, kinsmen, and extended family — a significant theological distinction regarding the 'brothers of Jesus' question.

Uses נכשלים (nikhshalim — 'stumbled/were offended', from כשל H3782 — 'to stumble'). This is the specific OT verb for stumbling over an obstacle (Lev 26:37, Isa 8:14-15 'He shall be... a stone of stumbling'). Greek σκανδαλίζω may itself derive from the Hebrew concept of מכשול (mikhshol — 'stumbling block'). The Hebrew is the original; the Greek is the loan-concept.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'son of a smith' (נפח — metalworker). Greek: 'the carpenter' (τέκτων — woodworker). Different professions.
Hebrew: 'his relatives' (קרובים — broad kinship). Greek: 'his brothers' (ἀδελφοί — siblings).
Hebrew: 'son of a smith AND Miriam' — names both parents. Greek: 'the son of Mary' — names only the mother.
translation_notes: 'Smith' for napach — the Isaiah 54:16 usage confirms this is a metalworker, not a woodworker. The distinction between Yeshua's father as a smith vs. a carpenter has theological implications: a smith works with fire and metal (judgment, refinement); a carpenter with wood (building, construction).
'Relatives' for qerovim preserves the Hebrew's broader kinship term, which does not require biological siblingship.
textual_notes: Isaiah 54:16: 'Behold, I have created the smith (נפח) who blows the coals in the fire and brings out a weapon for its purpose.' The same word for Yeshua's father's trade.

verses.translation: And Yeshua said{H559} to them: No prophet{H5030} is without{H1107} honor{H3519} except in his own land{H776} and among his acquaintances{H5234} and in his house{H1004}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מכיריו (makirav — 'his acquaintances/those who know him', from נכר H5234 — 'to recognize/know'). Greek has συγγενεῦσιν ('kinsmen'). A back-translator from 'kinsmen' would use קרוביו (qerovav — 'relatives') or משפחתו (mishpachto — 'family'). The Hebrew uses the recognition/knowledge verb — those who 'know' him can't see past their familiarity.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'his acquaintances' (מכיריו). Greek: 'his kinsmen' (συγγενεῦσιν). Familiarity vs. kinship.

verses.translation: And he did not wish{H7521} to do{H6213} any wonder{H6382} there, but a few{H4592} sick{H2470} ones he healed{H7495} by laying{H7760} hands{H3027} upon them.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew says he 'did not wish' (לא רצה) to do wonders. Greek says οὐκ ἐδύνατο ('was not able'). The Hebrew ascribes unwillingness; the Greek ascribes inability. A back-translator from 'could not' would write לא יכול (lo yakhol), not לא רצה (lo ratzah — 'did not want'). The Hebrew protects divine sovereignty — Yeshua chose not to act, rather than being unable.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'did not wish' (לא רצה — choice). Greek: 'could not' (οὐκ ἐδύνατο — inability). Fundamentally different theology of miracles.

verses.translation: For he marveled{H6382} at the scarcity of their faith{H539}. And he went around{H5437} the small{H6996} towns{H5892} teaching{H3925} and proclaiming{H1875}.

translation_notes: Uses both דורש (doresh — 'expounding', the Torah-study verb) and מלמד (melamed — 'teaching'). Two different Hebrew educational terms: דרש is interpretive exposition; למד is direct instruction.

verses.translation: And he called{H7121} the twelve disciples and sent{H7971} them two{H8147} by two{H8147}, and gave{H5414} them strength{H3581} to heal{H7495} all{H3605} the sick{H2470} and satan-possessed.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew gives the disciples authority over 'sick and satan-possessed' (חולים ומשוטנים). Greek specifies ἐξουσίαν τῶν πνευμάτων τῶν ἀκαθάρτων ('authority over unclean spirits'). Again, Hebrew uses שטן-theology where Greek uses spirit-impurity language. The Hebrew also pairs healing and deliverance as one commission.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: authority over 'sick and satan-possessed.' Greek: authority over 'unclean spirits' only. Hebrew has broader scope.

verses.translation: And he commanded{H6680} them that they should not carry{H5375} a sack or bread{H3899} or a stone or a belt{H2290}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew includes אבן (even — 'stone'). This may refer to a money-stone or weight used for transactions (cf. Deut 25:13 'you shall not have in your bag diverse stones/weights'). Greek has μὴ χαλκόν ('no copper/money'). A back-translator from 'money' would use כסף (kesef) or מעות (ma'ot), not אבן. The Hebrew preserves the ancient practice of carrying weight-stones for commerce.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'sack, bread, stone, belt.' Greek: 'bread, bag, money in belt' (ἄρτον, πήραν, χαλκόν εἰς τὴν ζώνην). Different items in different order.

verses.translation: But one scepter{H8275} in hand{H3027}, and sandals{H5275} of living leather on foot{H7272}, and they should not carry{H5375} two garments{H4403}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses שרביט (sharvit, H8275 — 'scepter'). This is the royal scepter — the word used in Esther 4:11, 5:2, 8:4 for the king's golden scepter that grants audience and authority. Greek has ῥάβδον ('rod/staff'). A back-translator from Greek would use מטה (mateh — 'staff') or מקל (maqel — 'stick'), not the royal scepter term. The Hebrew says the disciples carried scepters — symbols of royal authority — not mere walking sticks.

Uses עור חי (or chai — 'living leather') — untanned leather from freshly slaughtered animals. This specific material designation has no Greek equivalent; Greek says simply σανδάλια ('sandals'). The Hebrew specifies the material quality; the Greek names only the footwear type.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'scepter' (שרביט — royal authority). Greek: 'staff' (ῥάβδον — walking stick).
Hebrew: 'sandals of living leather.' Greek: just 'sandals.' Hebrew specifies material.
translation_notes: 'Scepter' for sharvit — the Esther connection (the king's scepter extending mercy and authority) may be intentional: the disciples carry the King's authority as they go out.

verses.translation: And he said{H559} to them: In whatever place{H4725} you come{H935}, there lodge{H3885} until you depart{H5265}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תלינו (talinu — 'you shall lodge', from לין H3885 — 'to lodge/spend the night'). This is the specific OT word for overnight hospitality (Gen 19:2, Judg 19:4,9,11,20, Ruth 1:16). Greek has μένετε ('remain/stay'). A back-translator would use שבו (shevu — 'stay'), not the hospitality verb לין.

Uses תסעו (tis'u — 'you depart/journey', from נסע H5265 — 'to pull up stakes/journey'). This is the Exodus travel verb — Israel 'journeyed' (ויסעו) from station to station (Ex 12:37, Num 10:12, 33:1ff). Greek has ἐξέλθητε ('go out'). The Hebrew frames the disciples' mission as an Exodus-like journeying.

verses.translation: And when they will not receive{H6901} you or hear{H8085} you, go out{H3318} from there and shake off{H5493} the dust{H6083} of your feet{H7272} as a testimony{H5715} against them.

translation_notes: Shaking off dust of the feet: a symbolic act marking separation from an unbelieving place, treating it as Gentile territory whose very soil defiles.

verses.translation: And they went{H1980} and proclaimed{H1875} that all should make repentance{H8666}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses תשובה (teshuvah — 'repentance/return', from שוב H7725 — 'to return'). The Hebrew concept of repentance is fundamentally about returning to YHWH — a physical and spiritual turning back (Deut 30:2, Isa 55:7, Hos 14:2, Joel 2:12). Greek μετανοέω means 'to change one's mind' — a cognitive reorientation. A back-translator from Greek 'change of mind' would use a cognitive verb, not the return/journey verb שוב. The Hebrew frames repentance as homecoming; the Greek frames it as mental revision.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'repentance/return' (תשובה — returning to God). Greek: μετανοέω ('change of mind'). Different root metaphors.
translation_notes: 'Repentance' for teshuvah — though conventional, this translation loses the movement inherent in שוב ('return'). Teshuvah is a journey back, not merely a changed opinion.
textual_notes: Hosea 14:2: 'Return (שובה), O Israel, to YHWH your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity.' The same root שוב defines the prophetic call to Israel.

verses.translation: And they healed the satan-possessed and cleansed{H4838} the sick{H2470} with an anointing{H4888} of blessed{H1288} oil{H8081}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses מישחת שמן מבורך (mishchat shemen mevorakh — 'anointing of blessed oil'). The root משח (mashach) is the same root that gives us משיח (Mashiach — 'the Anointed One'). Greek has ἤλειφον ἐλαίῳ ('anointed with oil'). Greek ἀλείφω is a common word for rubbing/smearing; Hebrew משח is the priestly-royal anointing verb (Ex 28:41, 30:30, 1 Sam 10:1, 16:13). A back-translator from Greek would use סכו בשמן (sakhu be-shemen — 'rubbed with oil'), not the messianic-priestly anointing term.
The oil is described as מבורך (mevorakh — 'blessed'). Greek has no equivalent adjective. The Hebrew implies the oil was ritually consecrated — paralleling the holy anointing oil of Exodus 30:25.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'anointing of blessed oil' (priestly/messianic). Greek: 'anointed with oil' (generic).
Hebrew: adds 'blessed' (מבורך). Greek: no qualification of the oil.

verses.translation: And when Herodos heard{H8085} — for the fame{H8088} of Yeshua was spread abroad — he said{H559} that Yochanan{H3110} the Immerser{H2881} has returned{H2421} alive{H2416} from the dead{H4194}, and therefore does wonders{H6382}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses טבול (tavul — 'the Immerser', from טבל H2881 — 'to dip/immerse'). This is the OT word for ritual immersion (2 Kings 5:14 where Naaman 'dipped' in the Jordan; Lev 4:6, 14:16). Greek has Βαπτιστής (Baptistēs — from βαπτίζω). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate as בפטיסטא. The Hebrew uses the native OT ritual-immersion vocabulary.

Uses פלאות (pela'ot — 'wonders', H6381) — the plural of the OT divine wonder-working term. Greek has δυνάμεις ('powers/mighty works'). A back-translator from Greek would use גבורות (gevurot — 'mighty deeds'), not the Exodus-wonder vocabulary.
translation_notes: 'Immerser' for tavul rather than 'Baptist' — preserving the Hebrew/OT ritual immersion concept rather than importing the Greek ecclesiastical title.

verses.translation: And others{H312} said{H559} that he is Eliyahu{H452}, and others said that he is a prophet{H5030} or one of the prophets{H5030}.
And when Herodos heard{H8085} this he said{H559}: This is Yochanan{H3110} whose head{H7218} I cut off{H3772}, and he has returned from death{H4194} to life{H2416}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חתכתי (chatakhti — 'I cut off', from כרת H3772 — 'to cut off/cut a covenant'). The root כרת is the OT word for both cutting a covenant (Gen 15:18, Ex 24:8) and being 'cut off' from the people as divine punishment (Gen 17:14, Ex 12:15, Lev 7:20). Greek has ἀπεκεφάλισα ('I beheaded'). A back-translator would transliterate or use a straightforward word. The Hebrew verb carries overtones of covenant-cutting — Herod 'cut off' the prophet in a grim inversion of covenant-making.

verses.translation: For this Herodos had seized{H8610} Yochanan{H3110} and placed him in the house of imprisonment{H5470}, on account of Herodis the wife{H802} of Philif his brother{H251}, whom he was holding.

one_way_hebrew: Uses בית הסוהר (beit ha-sohar — 'house of imprisonment', H5470). This is the same term used for Joseph's prison in Genesis 39:20-23 (בית הסהר). Greek has φυλακή ('guard/prison'). A back-translator from Greek would use more likely כלא (kele — 'prison') or משמר (mishmar — 'guard-house'). The Hebrew echoes the Joseph narrative — the righteous man imprisoned unjustly.
textual_notes: Genesis 39:20: 'And Joseph's master took him and put him in the prison (בית הסהר), the place where the king's prisoners were confined.' The same construction for Yochanan's imprisonment.

verses.translation: And Yochanan{H3110} said{H559} to Herodos: It is not fitting for you to hold{H2388} the wife{H802} of your brother{H251}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses אשת אחיך (eshet achikha — 'the wife of your brother'). This is verbatim Levitical language from Leviticus 18:16: 'You shall not uncover the nakedness of your brother's wife (ערות אשת אחיך)' and Leviticus 20:21. Greek uses the same construction (γυναῖκα τοῦ ἀδελφοῦ), but the Hebrew phrase carries the full weight of Levitical sexual prohibitions.
textual_notes: Leviticus 18:16, 20:21 — the prohibition against taking a brother's wife while the brother lives. Yochanan charges Herodos with violating Torah.

verses.translation: And Herodis despised him and laid in wait{H693} for him so that she could put him to death{H4191}, but she was not able{H3201}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ואורבו (ve-orevu — 'and laid in wait for him', from ארב H693 — 'to lie in ambush'). This is the specific OT word for ambush (Deut 19:11, Josh 8:2,4, Judg 9:25, Prov 1:11,18). Greek has ἐνεῖχεν αὐτῷ ('held a grudge against him'). A back-translator from 'held a grudge' would use שנאה (hatred) or נטרה (grudge), not the military-ambush verb. The Hebrew says Herodis plotted like a military ambusher.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'laid in wait' (ארב — ambush). Greek: 'held a grudge' (ἐνεῖχεν — bore resentment). Different intensity.

verses.translation: For Herodos held Yochanan{H3110} and considered{H2803} him holy{H6918} and righteous{H6662}, and guarded{H8104} him, and did many{H7227} things{H1697} for his sake, and heard{H8085} him willingly{H7522}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses קדוש וצדיק (qadosh ve-tsaddiq — 'holy and righteous') — the two great OT character attributes. Greek has ἄνδρα δίκαιον καὶ ἅγιον ('a righteous and holy man'). The order is reversed: Hebrew puts 'holy' first (God's attribute), then 'righteous' (human ethical attribute). Greek puts 'righteous' first. The Hebrew order mirrors OT priority where God's holiness precedes human righteousness.

verses.translation: And when the opportune days{H3117} drew near for Herodos, he made a feast{H2282} from his birth{H4138}, and invited{H2199} all the officers{H8269} of the thousands{H505} and the great{H1419} officers{H8269} from the Galil{H1551}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שרי האלפים (sarei ha-alafim — 'officers of the thousands'). This is the specific OT military rank from Moses' judicial system (Ex 18:21,25, Deut 1:15) and Israel's army structure (Num 31:14,48, 1 Sam 8:12, 22:7). Greek has χιλιάρχοις ('chiliarchs/tribunes'). While χιλίαρχος is a literal Greek calque, the Hebrew term carries the full weight of Israelite military-judicial tradition stretching back to Sinai.

Uses חג (chag, H2282 — 'feast/pilgrimage-festival'). This is the word for the three great pilgrimage festivals: Pesach, Shavuot, Sukkot (Ex 23:14, Deut 16:16). Greek has γενέσια ('birthday feast'). A back-translator from Greek would use a birthday-specific term. The Hebrew ironically labels Herod's debaucherous birthday as a chag — a sacred pilgrimage term.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'feast from his birth' (חג מלידתו — using the sacred festival term). Greek: γενέσια ('birthday celebration' — a Greco-Roman custom).

verses.translation: And the daughter of Herodis came{H935} in, twirling{H3769} before all the invited ones{H7121}, and it pleased{H3190} Herodos greatly{H3966} and all who were eating{H398}. And Herodos the king{H4428} said{H559} to the girl{H5291}: Ask{H7592} whatever you desire{H2654} and I will give{H5414} it to you.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מכרכרת (mekharkheret — 'twirling/whirling', from כרכר H3769). This is the exact word used in 2 Samuel 6:14,16 for David dancing/whirling before the ark: 'David was twirling (מכרכר) before YHWH with all his might.' Greek has ὀρχησαμένης ('having danced'). A back-translator from 'danced' would use רקדה (raqdah — 'danced') or חוללה (chollelah — 'danced in circle'). The Hebrew author uses the David-specific dance term — creating a dark inversion where Herodias's daughter twirls before a corrupt king as David twirled before YHWH.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'twirling' (מכרכרת — David's dance term). Greek: 'danced' (ὀρχέομαι — generic dancing).
translation_notes: 'Twirling' for mekharkheret — preserving the 2 Samuel 6 connection.
textual_notes: 2 Samuel 6:14: 'And David was twirling (מכרכר) before YHWH with all his might.' The same rare verb creates a deliberate contrast between sacred and profane dance.

verses.translation: And he made an oath{H7621} that he would give{H5414} her whatever she asked{H7592}, up to half{H2677} his kingdom{H4438}.

textual_notes: Echoes Esther 5:3,6, 7:2 where King Ahasuerus says to Esther: 'What is your request? Even to half the kingdom it shall be given you.' The Hebrew narrative frames Herod's oath in the language of the Esther story — but with inverted morality.

verses.translation: And when she went out from there, she said{H559} to her mother{H517}: What shall I ask{H7592}? And she said to her: Ask for the head{H7218} of Yochanan{H3110} the Immerser{H2881}.

And immediately she came{H935} to the king{H4428} and asked{H7592} him urgently, saying{H559}: I desire{H2654} that you give{H5414} me the head{H7218} of Yochanan{H3110} the Immerser{H2881} upon a simple wooden vessel{H6086}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses פשוטי כלי עץ (peshutei klei ets — 'simple wooden vessels'). Greek has ἐπὶ πίνακι ('on a platter/plate'). A back-translator from Greek would use קערה (qe'arah — 'dish/platter') or צלחת (tsalachat — 'plate'). The Hebrew specifies a crude wooden vessel — emphasizing the degradation and poverty of the instrument. The Hebrew vocabulary suggests Rabbinic legal language where פשוטי כלי עץ ('simple wooden vessels') is a halakhic category for vessels that do not receive impurity (Mishnah Kelim 15:1).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'simple wooden vessel' (crude, ritually significant). Greek: 'platter' (πίναξ — serving dish). Different object.

verses.translation: And the king{H4428} was grieved{H6087} on account of the oath{H7621} that he made and on account of the invited ones{H7121}, and did not wish to refuse her.
And he sent the executioner and commanded{H6680} him to bring{H5375} his head{H7218} upon one of the simple wooden vessels{H6086}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חתוך הראשים (chatokh ha-rashim — 'cutter of heads') for the executioner. This is a Hebrew compound title. Greek has σπεκουλάτωρ (spekoulator — a Latin loanword from speculator, a military executioner). A back-translator from Greek would transliterate the Latin military term. The Hebrew uses a native descriptive title instead.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'cutter of heads' (native Hebrew title). Greek: σπεκουλάτωρ (Latin military loanword). The Hebrew avoids the Latin term.

verses.translation: And he gave{H5414} it to the girl{H5291}, and the girl gave it to her mother{H517}.
And when his disciples knew{H3045} it, they came{H935} and took{H3947} his body{H1472}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'his body' (גופו). Greek: τὸ πτῶμα αὐτοῦ ('his corpse'). Hebrew uses the neutral 'body'; Greek uses the stronger 'corpse/fallen body.'

verses.translation: And the disciples came{H935} to Yeshua and told{H5608} him all{H3605} that they had done{H6213} and taught{H3925}.

And Yeshua said{H559}: Come{H935} and let us go{H1980} into the wilderness{H4057} and rest{H5117} a little{H4592}, for a great{H7227} people{H5971} was going{H1980} and returning{H7725}, and he had no leisure to eat{H398}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses נחו (nuchu — 'rest', from נוח H5117). Again the Noah/sabbath-rest verb. Yeshua calls his disciples to sabbath-rest in the wilderness — echoing Israel's wilderness rest (Ex 33:14 'My presence will go with you, and I will give you rest'). Greek has ἀναπαύσασθε ('rest yourselves'). The same general meaning, but the Hebrew verb carries Exodus and sabbath theology.

verses.translation: And they went up{H5927} in the small ship{H5600} and withdrew to a desolate{H2720} place{H4725}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses מקום חרב (maqom charev — 'desolate/ruined place'). The word חרב (charev) means 'dried up/desolate/ruined' and is the root of חרבה (chorbah — 'ruin') and חרב (cherev — 'sword'). It implies destruction and waste. Greek has ἔρημον τόπον ('deserted/uninhabited place') — neutral. A back-translator would use שומם (shomem — 'desolate') or just מדבר (midbar — 'wilderness'), not the ruins/destruction word חרב.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'desolate/ruined place' (חרב — destruction connotation). Greek: 'deserted place' (ἔρημος — merely empty).

verses.translation: And many{H7227} peoples{H5971} who saw{H7200} them recognized{H5234} him and followed{H4900} after him by way of land{H776} on foot{H7272}, and came{H935} from all{H3605} the towns{H5892}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses דרך ארץ לרגל (derekh erets la-regel — 'by way of land on foot'). This is a native Hebrew travel idiom. Greek has πεζῇ ('on foot'). The Hebrew triple construction (way + land + foot) is characteristically Hebraic phrasing that a back-translator would compress.

verses.translation: And when Yeshua came to land{H776} and saw{H7200} the people{H5971}, he had compassion{H7355} upon them, for they were like sheep{H6629} without{H1097} a shepherd{H7462}. And he began to teach{H3925} them many{H7227} and good{H2896} things{H1697}.

one_way_hebrew: DIRECT OT QUOTATION: כמו צאן בלא רועה ('like sheep without a shepherd') — from Numbers 27:17 where Moses asks YHWH to appoint a successor 'that the congregation of YHWH may not be like sheep that have no shepherd' (כצאן אשר אין להם רעה). Also 1 Kings 22:17 / 2 Chronicles 18:16. Greek has ὡς πρόβατα μὴ ἔχοντα ποιμένα — a fair translation of the Hebrew, but the Hebrew IS the original OT text. The Hebrew author naturally uses the Numbers 27 language; a Greek translator rendered it into Greek.

Uses ריחם (richem — 'had compassion', from רחם H7355 — 'womb/compassion'). This is womb-compassion — the deep visceral love of a mother for her child (Isa 49:15 'Can a woman forget her nursing child, that she should not have compassion (רחם) on the son of her womb?'). Greek ἐσπλαγχνίσθη (from σπλάγχνα — 'intestines') carries a similar visceral metaphor but from a different body organ.
translation_notes: 'Had compassion' for richem — the womb-love verb. Yeshua's response to the crowd is maternal in its depth.
textual_notes: Numbers 27:17: 'Let YHWH... appoint a man over the congregation... that the congregation of YHWH may not be like sheep that have no shepherd.' Moses' prayer for a successor — Joshua/Yeshua (same name) was the answer. The Hebrew Yeshua fulfills the role Moses prayed for.

verses.translation: And when the greater part of the day{H3117} had passed{H5674}, his disciples drew near{H7126} to him and said{H559}: This is a very desolate{H2720} place{H4725} and much{H7227} time{H8160} has passed.
Release{H5800} the peoples to go{H1980} to the small towns{H5892} around here and buy{H7069} food{H400} to eat{H398}.
And Yeshua answered{H6030} and said{H559} to them: You give{H5414} them to eat{H398}. Go then and buy{H7069} two hundred{H3967} loaves{H3603} of bread{H3899} and give{H5414} them to eat.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Hebrew says מאתים ככרות לחם (matayim kikrot lechem — 'two hundred loaves of bread'). Greek says δηναρίων διακοσίων ἄρτους ('two hundred denarii worth of bread'). The Hebrew gives a QUANTITY of bread (200 loaves); the Greek gives a PRICE (200 denarii). A back-translator from Greek would write 'bread of 200 denarii' using the monetary term דינר, not a count of loaves. The Hebrew counts bread; the Greek counts money. The Hebrew perspective is about provision; the Greek about cost.

ככרות (kikrot) — plural of ככר (kikkar, H3603). In the OT, ככר can mean both 'round loaf' (1 Sam 2:36, 10:3, Jer 37:21) and 'talent' (a weight/monetary unit, Ex 25:39). In context with לחם, it means 'loaves.' The word's monetary double-meaning may explain how the Greek came to render this as a monetary figure.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: '200 loaves of bread' (quantity). Greek: '200 denarii of bread' (price). Different measurement systems.

verses.translation: And Yeshua said{H559} to them: How many{H4100} loaves{H3899} do you have? Look{H5027} and see. And when they looked they said{H559}: We have five{H2568} loaves{H3899} and two{H8147} fish{H1709}.
And Yeshua commanded{H6680} that they seat{H3427} the people{H5971} and the companies upon the grass{H6212} [called pei].

one_way_hebrew: Uses חיילות (chaylot — 'companies/troops'). The word חיל (chayil) is a military term for an army unit, force, or troop (Ex 14:4, 1 Sam 17:20, 2 Sam 24:4). Greek has συμπόσια ('banquet-groups/drinking parties'). A back-translator from Greek would use חבורות (chavurot — 'groups') or מסיבות (mesivot — 'circles'). The Hebrew organizes the crowd in military formations — an echo of the wilderness camp order of Numbers 2.

The text adds a botanical annotation: [נקרא פי] ('called pei') — identifying the specific type of grass. This kind of local botanical notation is characteristic of an eyewitness or local author, not a translator.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'companies' (חיילות — military groupings). Greek: 'groups' (συμπόσια — banquet parties). Different organizational metaphor.
Hebrew includes botanical name of the grass. Greek has only χλωρῷ χόρτῳ ('green grass').

verses.translation: And they sat{H3427} by fifties{H2572} and by hundreds{H3967}.

one_way_hebrew: Hebrew order: fifties then hundreds. Greek order: hundreds then fifties (κατὰ ἑκατὸν καὶ κατὰ πεντήκοντα). Different ordering. The Hebrew matches the military organization of Exodus 18:21 where Moses appointed rulers of thousands, hundreds, fifties, and tens — listed from smallest upward in Hebrew style.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: fifties then hundreds (small to large). Greek: hundreds then fifties (large to small). Reversed order.
textual_notes: Exodus 18:21: 'rulers of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens.' The wilderness feeding mirrors the wilderness camp structure.

verses.translation: And Yeshua took{H3947} the five{H2568} loaves{H3899} and the two{H8147} fish{H1709} and made supplications and thanksgivings{H8426}, and broke{H1234} them and gave{H5414} them to his disciples to set{H5117} before them, and likewise divided{H2505} the two fish.

one_way_hebrew: Uses חינות והודאות (chinot ve-hoda'ot — 'supplications and thanksgivings'). חינות from חן (chen — 'grace/favor') — petitions for grace. הודאות from ידה (yadah — 'to give thanks/confess'). These are TWO distinct Hebrew liturgical acts. Greek has εὐλόγησεν ('blessed') — a single act. A back-translator from 'blessed' would write ברך (berakh — 'blessed'), not the double liturgical formula. The Hebrew preserves the two-part Jewish blessing structure: petition (bakashah) followed by thanksgiving (hodayah).
greek_deviations: Hebrew: two acts — 'supplications and thanksgivings' (חינות והודאות). Greek: one act — 'blessed' (εὐλόγησεν). Hebrew has fuller liturgical detail.

verses.translation: And they all{H3605} ate{H398} and were satisfied{H7646}.

translation_notes: שבעו (save'u — 'were satisfied', from שבע H7646). This is the Deuteronomic promise word: 'you will eat and be satisfied' (Deut 6:11, 8:10, 11:15). The wilderness feeding fulfills the Deuteronomic covenant blessing.
textual_notes: Deuteronomy 8:10: 'And you shall eat and be satisfied (ושבעת) and bless YHWH your God for the good land he has given you.' The feeding miracle echoes the manna narrative.

verses.translation: And they distributed{H2505} from the remainder{H3498} twelve{H8147}{H6240} baskets from what was left over{H3498} of the loaves{H3899} and the fish{H1709}.

translation_notes: Twelve baskets — one for each tribe of Israel. The surplus is a sign of covenant abundance.

verses.translation: And those who ate{H398} were five{H2568} thousand{H505} men{H376}.
And immediately he commanded{H6680} his disciples to enter{H935} the small ship{H5600} and to go{H1980} across{H5676} the waters{H4325} toward Bethsaida, while he sends{H7971} the people{H5971} away.

translation_notes: ביתה צידה (beitah tsidah) — literally 'house of provision/hunting.' The Hebrew preserves the Semitic meaning of Bethsaida.

verses.translation: And when his disciples went up{H5927} on the mountain{H2022}, he prayed{H6419} by himself{H905}.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'when his disciples went up on the mountain, he prayed by himself.' Greek: 'having sent them away, he went up on the mountain to pray.' In the Hebrew, the DISCIPLES go up the mountain; in Greek, YESHUA goes up. Different subjects.

verses.translation: And when evening{H6153} came, the small ship{H5600} was in the sea{H3220}, and Yeshua alone entered.

greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'Yeshua alone entered' — ambiguous. Greek: Yeshua was 'alone on the land' (μόνος ἐπὶ τῆς γῆς). Different location.

verses.translation: And Yeshua saw{H7200} them struggling{H6887} in rowing, for the wind{H7307} was against{H5048} them. And he came{H935} to them around the middle{H2677} of the night{H3915}, walking{H1980} upon the sea{H3220}.

one_way_hebrew: הולך על הים (holekh al ha-yam — 'walking upon the sea'). This echoes Job 9:8 where God alone 'treads upon the heights of the sea' (דורך על במתי ים). Also Psalm 77:20: 'Your way was through the sea, your path through the great waters.' By walking on the sea, Yeshua performs an act that the OT attributes exclusively to YHWH. The Hebrew reader immediately recognizes the divine action.
textual_notes: Job 9:8: 'Who alone stretched out the heavens and treads upon the heights of the sea (דורך על במתי ים).' Walking on the sea is a YHWH-exclusive prerogative in the OT.

verses.translation: They thought he was some evil{H7451} spirit{H7307} and they all{H3605} cried out{H6817}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses רוח רעה (ruach ra'ah — 'evil spirit'). This is the specific OT term from 1 Samuel 16:14-16,23, 18:10, 19:9 — 'an evil spirit from YHWH' that tormented Saul. Greek has φάντασμα ('phantom/ghost'). A back-translator from Greek would use a word for ghost/apparition, not the 1 Samuel theological term. The Hebrew frames the disciples' fear through Saul's torment narrative.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'evil spirit' (רוח רעה — 1 Samuel term). Greek: 'phantom' (φάντασμα — Hellenistic ghost concept).

verses.translation: And they were troubled{H943}. And Yeshua immediately cried{H2199} out and said{H559}: Stand firm in confidence — I am He{H589}{H1931} — do not fear{H3372}.

one_way_hebrew: CRITICAL: Uses אני הוא (ani hu — 'I am He'). This is the divine self-identification formula from Isaiah: 'I, I am He' (אני אני הוא, Deut 32:39); 'I am He' (אני הוא, Isa 41:4, 43:10,13, 46:4, 48:12). YHWH uses אני הוא to declare his unique identity. Greek ἐγώ εἰμι also carries this weight (cf. John 8:58), but the Hebrew formula directly connects to the Isaiah/Deuteronomy declarations. Yeshua, walking on the sea (a YHWH act, Job 9:8), then declares 'I am He' (a YHWH formula). The Hebrew audience hears two interlocking divine claims.
translation_notes: 'I am He' for ani hu — preserving the divine self-identification formula. Not merely 'it is I' (self-identification) but 'I AM HE' (divine declaration).

'Stand firm in confidence' for imdu be-vitchah — the Hebrew doesn't merely say 'take courage' (θαρσεῖτε) but 'stand firm in trust/security.' The root בטח (H983) is the OT word for trusting in YHWH (Ps 4:6, 9:11, 21:8, 25:2).
textual_notes: Isaiah 43:10: 'You are my witnesses, declares YHWH, and my servant whom I have chosen, that you may know and believe me and understand that I am He (אני הוא). Before me no god was formed, nor shall there be any after me.'

verses.translation: And then he went up{H5927} with them into the ship{H5600}, and the wind{H7307} stood still{H5975}. And they were even more amazed{H8539}.
For still{H5750} they did not recognize{H5234} the wonder{H6382} of the five{H2568} loaves{H3899}, for their heart{H3820} was clouded.

one_way_hebrew: Uses ערפליי (arafliy — 'clouded/foggy'). The root ערפל (arafel) is the word for the thick cloud/darkness that surrounds God's presence on Sinai (Ex 20:18, Deut 4:11, 5:19, 2 Sam 22:10, Ps 18:10). Greek has πεπωρωμένη ('hardened/petrified'). A back-translator from 'hardened' would use מוקשה (muqshah) or מאובנת (me'ubenet). The Hebrew says their hearts were in arafel-darkness — the same darkness that shrouded Sinai. They stood in the presence of divine glory but could not see through the cloud.
greek_deviations: Hebrew: 'clouded' (ערפליי — Sinai-theophany darkness). Greek: 'hardened' (πεπωρωμένη — petrified). Different metaphors with different theological associations.
textual_notes: Exodus 20:18: 'And the people stood far off, while Moses drew near to the thick darkness (ערפל) where God was.' The disciples' clouded hearts echo Israel's inability to approach God's presence.

verses.translation: And when they crossed{H5674} over, they came{H935} to the land{H776} of Ginnesaret.
When he went out{H3318} from the ship{H5600}, immediately they recognized{H5234} Yeshua.

And they hastened{H4116} throughout all{H3605} the land{H776} to bring{H935} the sick{H2470} on beds{H4296} wherever they heard{H8085} he was. In whatever city{H5892} or province he entered{H935}, they passed through the ways{H1870} and implored{H2470} him that they might only touch{H5060} the edge{H8193} of his garment{H4403}, for all{H3605} who touched{H5060} were healed{H7495}.

one_way_hebrew: Uses שפת מלבושו (sfat malvusho — 'the lip/edge of his garment', H8193). שפה means 'lip/edge/border.' This echoes Numbers 15:38-39 where God commands Israel to make fringes (ציצית) on the corners/edges (כנפי) of their garments. Greek has τοῦ κρασπέδου τοῦ ἱματίου ('the fringe/border of his garment'). The Hebrew term 'lip' (שפה) for the garment edge is a distinctly Hebrew construction.
translation_notes: This verse merges what Greek separates as vv55-56. The Hebrew source combines both verses into a single narrative unit.
textual_notes: The touching of the garment's edge recalls the woman with the blood flow (5:27-28) and connects to the tsitsit (fringes) of Numbers 15:38-39, which remind Israel of YHWH's commandments.

chapter_notes.summary: Mark 6 in Hebrew contains numerous strong one-way markers. The most significant: (1) בן נפח ('son of a smith/forger') where Greek has 'carpenter' — entirely different professions, with נפח (Isa 54:16) being a metalworker; (2) קרוביו ('his relatives') where Greek has 'brothers' — using the broader kinship term; (3) מאתים ככרות לחם ('200 loaves of bread') where Greek has '200 denarii worth of bread' — Hebrew counts bread, Greek counts money; (4) מכרכרת ('twirling' — 2 Sam 6:14 David's dance term) for Herodias's daughter where Greek has generic 'danced'; (5) שרביט ('scepter' — Esther's royal term) where Greek has 'staff'; (6) חיילות ('military companies') for seating where Greek has 'banquet groups'; (7) ערפליי ('clouded' — Sinai's thick darkness) for the disciples' hearts where Greek has 'hardened'; (8) אני הוא ('I am He' — Isaiah's divine self-identification) on the sea; (9) חינות והודאות ('supplications and thanksgivings') for the blessing where Greek has single 'blessed'; (10) פשוטי כלי עץ ('simple wooden vessels') for the platter — halakhic terminology; (11) תשובה ('return') for repentance; (12) שטן-theology continuing throughout. The chapter also contains a verbatim OT quote (כמו צאן בלא רועה — 'like sheep without a shepherd,' Num 27:17) and multiple echoes of Exodus wilderness narratives in the feeding account.
